text: Functions: their parts, return values, order, and reusable helpers.
A **function** packs a computation under a name. You write the logic once, test it once, and call it as often as you like.
Calling it jumps into the body with the arguments copied into the parameters. It runs until return, and hands back one value.
Write the side length once as a function instead of copying the formula three times (P5735). One fix in the function fixes every call.
A function that returns nothing has type `void`. A function must be declared above the code that calls it.
Calling a function defined **below** main, with no declaration above, gives "was not declared in this scope". Put helpers above main, or declare them first.
A non void function must return on every path. Falling off the end returns garbage, and the compiler only warns.
A **lambda**, `[](int x) { return x * x * x; }`, is a small unnamed function written where it is used. You met one as the comparison in sort.
Small yes or no helpers make the main loop read like the statement.
A bool helper can return as soon as the answer is known: `return false` inside the loop stops the whole function.
`vector<int>` is an array that grows with `push_back` and knows its `size()`. Handy when you do not know the count in advance (P5736, P5737).
Once isPrime exists, "write each even number as a sum of two primes, smallest first" is two loops and one test (P1304).
Reuse helpers across problems: the same isPrime solves P5736, P1304, P1217 and P1075. Keep a tested copy in your notes.

title: 变量作用域与参数传递

text: Copies or references, arrays as parameters, and where a name lives.
By default a parameter is a **copy**: changing it inside does not touch the caller. Add `&` to make it a **reference**, another name for the caller's variable.
Use `&` to change arguments (swap) or to send back several results. Use `const string &s` to pass a big object without copying it and without changing it.
An array argument is **never copied**: the function works on the caller's array. Pass the length n along with it, and write const when it should only read.
A local with the same name as a global **hides** it. Give globals clear names. `::cnt` reaches the global when you must.
Base case, smaller call, call stack, and memoisation.
A recursive function has a **base case** that answers directly, and a **recursive case** that calls itself on a smaller input. Each call waits on a stack until the call it made returns.
No base case, or a step that does not shrink the input, means infinite recursion: a stack overflow crash. Very deep recursion, around 10⁵ to 10⁶ levels, can crash too.
Recursion fits when the answer for n is built from the answer for a smaller n (P5739, P5743). Any such recursion can also be a loop: recursion is shorter, the loop avoids deep stacks.

title: Divide into parts: a recursive picture

text: Split the square into four quarters. One is handled directly; the other three are **the same problem at half size**. The function describes one level, and recursion repeats it (P5461).
Plain `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` recomputes the same values again and again: hopeless for n = 50.
Store each result the first time and return it straight away next time. Each fib(k) is then computed once: O(n). This "remember results" idea is the seed of dynamic programming.
Some answers need no recursion at all: the sum over all subsets is (sum of elements) × 2ⁿ⁻¹, because each element is in half of the subsets (P2415).
Group fields, member functions, arrays of structs, and sorting them.
A **struct** is a new type made of named fields. One Student carries a name and three scores together, so sorting moves the whole record at once.
Fields use a dot: `s.name`. An array of structs, `Student a[1005]`, is a table with one row per student.
Using `>`, not `>=`, when searching for the best keeps the **first** student among ties (P5740). `Student &s = a[best]` gives a short name without copying.
The pair loop from chapter 5 works unchanged on structs (P5741).
Pass a struct by reference, `Person &p`, when the function should update it, and by `const Person &p` when it only reads. Passing by value copies every field.
`score * 1.2` uses floating point and can land just below the true value. `score * 6 / 5` stays exact in integers (P5744, P5742).
`sort(a, a + n, cmp)` calls `cmp(x, y)` to ask "must x come before y?". Compare the main key first; only on a tie, compare the next key.
cmp must be a **strict** order: return false when x and y are equal. Writing `>=` instead of `>` can crash sort.
Or give the struct an `operator<` and call plain `sort(a, a + n)`. For a one off order, a lambda works too.
C has no references or member functions. It passes addresses with `&x` and works through pointers with `*`, and sorts with qsort.
